Cu3P/C Nanocomposites for Efficient Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction and Zn–CO2 Battery
Mingyue Peng1 2, Suqin Ci1 ∗, Ping Shao1 2, Pingwei Cai2, and Zhenhai Wen1 2 ∗ 1Key Laboratory of Jiangxi Province for Persistent Pollutants Control and Resources Recycle,
Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang 330063, China 2CAS (Chinese Academy of Sciences) Key Laboratory of Design and Assembly of Functional Nanostructures,
Fujian Provincial Key Laboratory of Nanomaterials, Fujian Institute of Research on the Structure of Matter, Fuzhou, Fujian 350002, China
Exploiting effective electrocatalysts toward electrochemical conversion of CO2 into valued-added chemicals is highly desirable for achieving the global carbon cycle. In this work, we report the synthesis of Cu3P/C nanocomposites by phosphatizing the copper-based metal organic framework precursor. Systematic electrochemical characterizations demonstrate the Cu3P/C nanocomposites hold high activity and favorable selectivity towards CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) into CO, as manifested by an onset potential is about−0.25 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) and a faradic efficiency (FE) of 47% for CO production at a relatively low potential (−0.3 V). The attractive catalytic properties might be attributed to the synergistic effect of cooper and phosphorus elements, as well as the unique structure of Cu3P. Furthermore, we propose an asymmetrical-electrolyte Zn–CO2 battery with the Cu3P/C as cathode catalyst, demonstrating a decent performance with an open-circuit voltage of 1.5 V and a power density of 2.6 mW cm−2 (at 10 mA cm−2).
Keywords: CO2 Electrochemical Reduction, Cu3P/C Nanocomposites, Electrocatalysis, MOF Derived Materials, Zn–CO2 Battery.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Fossil fuels, as the current dominant global energy sources, play a critical role in the current industrial development due to their easy availability, versatility, and high energy density.1–3 However, the over-consumption of fossil fuels, associated with CO2 releasing, leads to increased concerns in energy risk and global warming as well as a series of serious problems.4 Carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) has been proposed to be a promising technology for pacifying these anxieties with potential conversion of CO2 into value-added products.
3 5 However, CO2RR is a complicated process with multiple proton and electron transfer steps, and the products are diversified from gaseous carbon monoxide, methane, ethylene, acetylene to liquid products like formic acid, formaldehyde, methanol, ethanol, etc.1 Thus, it is highly desirable to develop an efficient and good-selectivity electrocatalyst for degradation or resource utilization of CO2, in the hope to achieve ideal global carbon cycle.6

Up to now, a variety of materials have been exploited as electrocatalyst toward CO2RR, including metallic alloys, transition metals, transition metal dichalcogenides, metals organic complexes, heteroatom-doped carbon, and metal organic frameworks (MOFs).7 8 Recent studies suggest that copper and its derivatives are the most attractive materials as electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction.
9 10 On the other hand, MOFs with porous structure exhibit exceptionally high specific surface area that are beneficial for improving activity sites.11 Moreover, direct carbonization of MOFs offers a simple approach to manufacture the functional cooper/porous carbon composite materials with enhanced electric conductivity and stability. Actually, various Cu-based composites, including copper/carbon, copper oxides/carbon and copper phosphides/carbon hybrids, have been developed with copper organic frameworks (HKUST-1)12 as precursor; they manifest favorable electrochemical properties for potential applications in fields of supercapacitor materials13 and hydrogen evolution catalysts.14 However, there are still rare reports in developing MOFs-derived materials as electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction reaction.

Herein, we demonstrate the preparation of Cu3P/C via a one-step phosphorizing of HKUST-1. The as-derived Cu3P/C nanocomposites exhibit improved selectivity for CO from CO2 at a lower overpotential compared with that of HKUST-1. In addition, we set up a novel asymmetricelectrolyte Zn–CO2 cell, in which the Cu3P/C loading on carbon cloth was used as cathode for CO2RR catalysis in 0.1 M KHCO3 and Zn plate was applied as anode in 4.0 M NaOH, respectively. A bipolar membrane was used for separating chambers of cathode and anode. The asproposed Zn–CO2 cell can not only catalysis the reduction of CO2 into CO, but generate electricity energy with enhanced open circuit voltage and power density.

sections.heading: 2.1. Chemicals and Materials
sections.text: All the chemical reagents were analytical pure grade and were used without further treatment. Benzene-1,3,5tricarboxylic acid, copper(II) nitrate hydrate (Cu(NO3 2 · 3H2O) and sodium hypophosphite (NaH2PO2 were purchased from Aladdin Industrial Corporation, N ,N - dimethylformamide (DMF), ethanol and potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3 were purchased from Sinopharm Group CO. Ltd. Nafion solution (5%) was obtained from Dupont.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Synthesis of HKUST-1:
sections.text: HKUST-1 was used as a precursor for Cu/C and Cu3P/C materials that it was synthesized by a general approach described by Yaghi et al.12 Benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid (1.8 g, 24 mmol) and copper(II) nitrate hydrate (3.6 g, 43 mmol) were dissolved for 20 min in 90 mL of solvent consisting of equal parts N ,N -dimethylformamide, ethanol and deionized water. Then mixed solution was transferred to a Teflon-lined autoclave and kept at 85 C for 20 h. Sediment was rinsed with DMF, the product was immersed in dichloromethane for 3 d and washed three times, finally, removed under vacuum at 170 C.15

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Synthesis of Cu3P/Carbon Materials
sections.text: The above precursor HKUST-1 was phosphorized by using NaH2PO2 under Ar flow. The HKUST-1 (0.4 g) and NaH2PO2 (1.6 g) were placed separately in a fused silica tube with the NaH2PO2 under the upstream side. Then the fused silica tube was heated to 350 C with a heating rate of 2 C min−1.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization
sections.text:
XRD spectra were obtained by using a Desktop X-ray Diffractometer using Cu K radiation. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was recorded on a Hitachi S-4800 microscope. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and elemental X-ray analysis (EDX) distribution were performed on a FE-TEM
(Tecnai F20). The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was measured using a Thermo ESCALAB 250 Xi instrument with monochromatic Al k line.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical Experiments
sections.text: Electrochemical CO2 reduction measurements were performed on in a three-electrode system, with the catalysts modified electrodes as a working electrode, platinum mesh as a counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl a reference electrode. All electrochemical tests occurred in H-type electrolytic cell (10 mL) with separating cathode chamber and the anode chamber using a proton exchange membrane (Nafion 112). The cathodic compartment was continuously bubbled with 20 cm2 S−1 CO2 and was connected a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2014 Instruments) for quantity and quality analysis of catalytic products.

sections.heading: 2.5. Zn–CO2 Cell Tests
sections.text: For fabrication of the asymmetrical-electrolyte Zn-air battery, the cathode chamber was filled with 0.1 M CO2saturated NaHCO3, while the anode chamber was containing 4.0 M NaOH. A bipolar membrane was position between the anode and the cathode chamber to hinder direct mixing of NaHCO3 and NaOH. The Cu3P/C loading on carbon cloth with 1 mg cm−2 was applied as cathode to catalysis CO2 reduction reaction in 0.1 M NaHCO3 solution, accompanying with the oxidation of Zn in 4.0 M NaOH solution. The open circuit voltage (OCV) and discharge polarization cure (LSV) were collected on CHI 660E workstation.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Figures 1(a), (b) show the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the HKUST-1 and the Cu3P/C, respectively. The HKUST-1 exhibits a uniform octahedral morphology and the Cu3P/C catalyst consists of flower-like microstructure. High-resolution transition electron microscopy (HRTEM) image (Fig. 1(c)) indicates that the Cu3P/C has a well-defined crystalline structure with identified lattice spaces of 0.25 nm and 0.23 nm, corresponding to the (112) and (202) plane of Cu3P, respectively. The MOF precursor and the evolved product are investigated by using X-ray powder diffraction (XRD), which indicates that the MOF shows a similar XRD pattern to the simulated spectrum.16 The further phosphization treatment successfully induce the conversion of HKUST-1 into Cu3P, as evidenced by the corresponding XRD with the six characteristic diffraction peaks of Cu3P at 36.2
, 39.3 , 41.8 , 45.0 , 46.5 , and 47.3 , corresponding to (112), (202), (211), (300), (113) and (212) crystalline planes (JCPDS02-1263), respectively (Fig. 1(d)).17
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is measured to study the types of element and valence status between elements. Figure 1(e) exhibits the survey spectra of the

One can clearly observe the XPS spectrum of Cu 2p for the Cu3P/C has four main peaks that the peak at 932.8 eV, 952.8 eV, 935.4 eV and 955.5 eV, which belong to the Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 of Cu–P and Cu1+ states or Cu2+ states, respectively. In addition, the other two satellite peaks at 944.2 eV and 963.1 eV are described as the +2 oxidation state of the surface of copper, which could be caused by oxidation for air contact. The peaks at 128.8 eV, 129.6 eV and 134.2 eV for high resolution P 2p XPS
spectrum of the Cu3P/C samples can be assigned to the P 2p3/2, P 2p1/2 and the oxidation state of P for the surface species (Fig. 1(f)), further confirming the oxidation on the surface of Cu–P.17 18
Electrochemical tests were performed to estimate the catalytic activity of Cu3P/C for CO2 reduction. Figure 2(a) presents the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of the Cu3P/C and the HKUST-1 samples in N2 and CO2saturated 0.1 M KHCO3. The Cu3P/C catalyst manifests

an onset potential of about −0.25 V for CO2 reduction, which is more positive than the HKUST-1 electrode that shows an onset potential of about −0.45 V. Additionally, the current density of the Cu3P/C can reach 1 mA cm −2 at −400 mV (vs. RHE), this value is also lower than these of HKUST-1 (−471 mV). These results demonstrate the Cu3P/C catalyst has decent electrochemical activities towards CO2RR. As shown in Figure 2(b), the Cu3P/C possesses a lower charge-transfer resistance than HKUST-1, implying that the Cu3P/C can facilitate electron transfer for CO2 reduction and have more prominent activities than the HKUST-1 precursor. The varied distribution of the gaseous products at different potentials from −0.3 V to −1.0 V (vs. RHE) were plotted for the HKUST-1 and the Cu3P/C catalysts (Fig. 2(c)). The Cu3P/C composites were proved to show a maximum faradic efficiency (FE) of CO with around 47% at −0.3 V. In addition, the major products are CO and H2 with a tunable ratio depending on the applied potential, thus enabling the possibility for FischerTropsch manufacture liquid hydrocarbons with these products by adjusting the applied potential. Figure 2(d) records the variation of the current density corresponding to the CO2 reduction and the FEs of CO at a fixed potential of −0.3 V, the Cu3P/C exhibits a rather stable current density of ∼0.05 mA cm−2 with an average CO FE of ∼47%. The values of FE have a small fluctuation upon operating time, which can be attributed to the effects of CO2 bubbling during testing.19
To evaluate the applicability of Cu3P/C catalyst, we put forward a concept of aqueous Zn–CO2 battery, in which
the CO2 reduction reaction was designed at cathode side to replace the oxygen reduction reaction in a conventional Zn-air battery. Figure 3(a) displays the schematic illustration of the battery device, in which a Zn plate was used as the anode and the Cu3P/C-coated carbon cloth was applied as the cathode. The anodic reaction is electrochemical oxidation of Zn, which provides the electron passing through the outer circuit to the cathode for the cathodic reaction, i.e., electrochemical reduction of CO2. Figure 3(b) records the open circuit voltage of the Zn–CO2 battery, which can afford a stable open-circuit voltage of 1.5 V. The polarization curve and the corresponding power density of a single Zn–CO2 battery are shown in Figure 3(c), from which one can observe a maximum power density of 2.6 mW cm−2 can be achieved at current density of 10 mA cm−2. We also demonstrate Zn–CO2 batteries with the Cu3P/C CO2 as cathode can be used as the power, as exemplified by Figure 3(d), which prove that three series connected Zn– CO2 batteries based on the Cu3P/C cathode can power two small red light-emitting diode (LED) with an excellent stability before anodic Zn foils exhausted.20–22

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSION
sections.text:
In summary, the Cu3P/C composites are synthesized by a facile method and show potential as excellent catalyst for CO2RR with high selectivity, a relatively low onset potential, and low cost. Compared to HKUST-1, the Cu3P/C can achieve a high faradic efficiency of about 47% for CO at a relatively lower potential. The primary Zn–CO2 battery is proposed with the Cu3P/C as cathode, demonstrating
